To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NPI licensing in German is subject to a number of restrictions which can be described in terms of an HPSG architecture.

(a) NPI licensing contexts in German can be divided into three classes, namely, downward-entailing, non-monotonic and non-entailing contexts, (b) there are NPIs which are restricted to downward-entailing contexts (DE-NPIs), and there are NPI-licensing contexts which are restricted to DE-NPIs, (c) there are NPs which are restricted to non-monotonic contexts (non-monotonic NPIs),
NPIs are subject to a number of distributional restrictions which are best captured in terms of a semantic theory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: What are the semantic, syntactic and pragmatic properties of NPIs and what is the role of NPIs in a theory of grammar?
the following questions: (1) What are the properties of NPIs in German?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single licensing context for NPIs.
the distributional restrictions on NPI licensing are not fully understood, and that there is still room for further research.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NPI licensing theory presented here is the first attempt to provide an account of the data in terms of HPSG.

the NPI licensing theory presented in this article can be viewed as a first attempt to integrate the semantic theories of Ladusaw and Fauconnier, and the syntactic theories of Horn, Krifka, and Linebarger, within HPSG.

we are able to provide a formal account of NPIs in German which (a) is compatible with the general framework of HPSG, (b) is based on a theory which is empirically adequate, and (c) which can be easily integrated into a larger theory of German syntax.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a semantic theory of NPI licensing can be integrated into HPSGrules and that it can be used in an HPSG grammar for German to derive the distributional properties of NPIs in a principled way.

NPI licensing is a matter of the interaction of several grammatical properties of the context and of the NPI itself, and that this interaction is captured by a set of constraints which are defined in terms of the properties in question.
NPIs are not licensed in all DE contexts.
